title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI can safely and effectively support student learning in real classroom tutoring contexts, addressing a central question for scaling one-to-one instruction: can an AI tutor deliver benefits comparable to human tutors without compromising pedagogical quality or safety? The authors focus on LearnLM, a generative AI model fine-tuned for pedagogical dialogue, and test it in an exploratory randomized controlled trial in UK secondary school mathematics classrooms.

The intervention was embedded in the Eedi mathematics platform. Students who made an initial mistake on a diagnostic question were randomly assigned either to receive a static pre-written hint or to enter an interactive tutoring session. Within the tutoring condition, sessions were further randomized to human tutor alone versus LearnLM supervised by a human tutor who could approve, edit, or replace every drafted message before it reached the student. The study involved 165 students in Years 9 and 10 (ages 13–15) across five UK secondary schools, supported by 17 expert tutors, and ran for seven weeks in May–June 2025.

Results suggest that supervised LearnLM was safe, with tutors approving most drafted messages and finding no harmful content in the audited corpus. In terms of learning, interactive tutoring outperformed static hints on immediate remediation and misconception resolution, while LearnLM performed about as well as human tutors on those near-term outcomes. Most notably, LearnLM produced stronger knowledge transfer to the next topic than human tutors alone, suggesting a possible advantage for AI-supported tutoring in promoting durable learning. The paper concludes that pedagogically constrained genAI systems may be promising for scalable individualized support, though longer-term studies and broader subject areas are still needed.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a well-designed exploratory randomized controlled trial with student-level randomization and a nested tutoring-session randomization, which gives strong causal evidence. Confidence is tempered by the small sample size, short duration, and the fact that LearnLM was human-supervised, so it is not a fully autonomous ChatGPT-style tutoring test.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed learning effects are modest to moderate in practical terms, with a 5.5 percentage point transfer advantage over human tutoring and strong immediate correction rates. The intervention targets a priority K-12 population in secondary mathematics, but the evidence is early-stage and based on a constrained, supervised deployment.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI math tutoring in chat-based sessions on the Eedi platform, using LearnLM/Gemini 2.0 Flash fine-tuned for pedagogy to draft Socratic responses that a human tutor supervises before sending to secondary students.
Static, pre-written misconception-specific hints delivered by the Eedi platform after an incorrect answer, used as the control/comparator condition.

finding.finding_summary: This exploratory RCT (n=165 Year 9-10 students across five UK secondary schools) found that supervised LearnLM tutoring was at least as effective as human tutoring for immediate math learning and better for transfer. Students guided by LearnLM solved the same missed question on the second attempt 93.0% of the time versus 91.2% for human tutors, and they were 66.2% successful on the first question of the next unit versus 60.7% for human tutors, a 5.5 percentage point advantage.
finding.measure: Second-attempt correctness on the same question; misconception resolution within the unit; transfer to the first question of the next study unit
finding.effect_size: 5.5 percentage points for transfer vs human tutors alone

finding.finding_summary: Compared with static pre-written hints, interactive tutoring produced substantially better immediate math correction and misconception resolution. Human tutoring yielded 91.2% second-attempt correctness versus 65.4% with static hints, and 94.9% resolved misconceptions versus 86.8% with static hints; supervised LearnLM was similarly strong at 93.0% and 95.4%, respectively.
finding.measure: Second-attempt correctness; misconception resolution within the study unit
finding.confidence_interval: Human tutoring 91.2% [88.5%, 93.6%] vs static hints 65.4% [63.8%, 66.9%]; LearnLM 93.0% [90.4%, 95.3%] vs static hints 65.4%; misconception resolution human 94.9% [92.6%, 96.8%] vs static 86.8% [85.7%, 88.0%]; LearnLM 95.4% [93.1%, 97.1%]

finding.finding_summary: Student survey responses suggested that interactive tutoring was perceived as more helpful than static hints. Among n=27 student respondents, interactive tutoring received an average helpfulness rating of 3.9/5 [3.1, 4.7] compared with 3.6/5 [2.9, 4.2] for static hints, though the paper frames this as a modest and suggestive signal rather than a primary outcome.
finding.confidence_interval: Interactive tutoring 3.9 [3.1, 4.7] vs static hints 3.6 [2.9, 4.2]; posterior probability of advantage 74.9%

finding.finding_summary: Tutors reported that supervising LearnLM made tutoring feel more fluid and efficient, with 82.4% selecting 'supporting multiple students at the same time' as the most useful feature. The paper also reports that tutor comfort with AI rose from 3.4 [2.9, 4.0] to 3.9 [3.3, 4.4] out of 5, with a posterior probability of increase of 90.0%, but it does not provide a rigorous throughput estimate.
finding.measure: Tutor survey responses; self-reported AI comfort; qualitative interview themes
finding.confidence_interval: AI comfort increase: 3.4 [2.9, 4.0] to 3.9 [3.3, 4.4]; posterior probability of increase 90.0%
